events.title: ActionScript 1.0 debuts with Flash 5
events.summary: Macromedia Flash 5 launched with ActionScript 1.0 — a JavaScript-like ECMAScript-based language for rich web media.
events.about: ActionScript was the programming language inside Flash — build browser games, video players, interactive ads, and animated sites. Famous era: Newgrounds flash games, early YouTube-era players, and corporate sites with splash intros. Syntax resembled JavaScript; code lived inside `.fla` authoring files.

narrative.whyChosen: ActionScript powered a decade of browser games, video players, and interactive sites before HTML5.
narrative.whyImportant: It was the first fully implemented, ECMAScript-based scripting layer in a mass-market authoring tool.
narrative.problemSolved: Flash 4 scripting was limited; Flash 5 needed a real language for complex client-side logic.

events.title: SQLite 1.0 released
events.summary: Richard Hipp released SQLite 1.0 on August 17, 2000 — a self-contained, serverless SQL database engine in a single C library.
events.about: SQLite embeds in apps, browsers, and phones — no separate server process. iOS, Android, Firefox, and countless desktop apps store data in `.sqlite` files. Teams use it for local caches, mobile offline sync, and tests. Example: a mobile app persisting user settings with `SELECT` and transactions without running Postgres.

narrative.whyChosen: SQLite made SQL available everywhere a C library could link — not just on database servers.
narrative.whyImportant: It is likely the most widely deployed database engine on earth, hidden inside applications.
narrative.problemSolved: Embedded apps needed relational storage without the complexity of client/server database administration.

events.title: CMake released
events.summary: Kitware introduced CMake on August 31, 2000 — a cross-platform build system generator for C and C++ projects.
events.about: CMake reads `CMakeLists.txt` files and emits Makefiles, Ninja files, or IDE projects — one build description for Linux, macOS, and Windows. It powers LLVM, KDE, OpenCV, and countless native libraries. Example: `cmake -B build && cmake --build build` configures and compiles without hand-writing platform-specific make rules.

narrative.whyChosen: CMake solved cross-platform native builds when autotools and Visual Studio projects diverged.
narrative.whyImportant: It became the de facto build meta-system for open-source C/C++ and influenced Conan and vcpkg workflows.
narrative.problemSolved: Maintaining separate build files per OS was unmaintainable for large C++ codebases like medical imaging toolkits.

events.title: Linus Torvalds: "Talk is cheap. Show me the code."
events.summary: Linus Torvalds dismisses architecture debates on the Linux kernel mailing list — ship patches, not opinions.
events.about: The line became open-source culture in eight words. It appears on stickers, README files, and every thread where design docs pile up without a pull request.

narrative.whyChosen: The motto of meritocratic open-source contribution.
narrative.whyImportant: It reinforced Linux's patch-driven governance over specification committees.
narrative.problemSolved: Mailing-list theory needed a norm that rewarded working implementations.

events.quoteText: Talk is cheap. Show me the code.

events.title: Joel Spolsky publishes the Joel Test
events.summary: Joel Spolsky's blog post The Joel Test lists twelve yes-or-no questions that separate great software teams from dysfunctional ones.
events.about: The Joel Test was never scientific — Joel admitted as much — but it spread because it was memorable and actionable. Teams still score themselves out of 12 in onboarding docs and engineering blog posts.

narrative.whyChosen: The most shared team-health checklist of the blog era.
narrative.whyImportant: It gave non-engineers a simple rubric for software organization quality.
narrative.problemSolved: Startups had no quick way to audit whether their dev process was broken.

events.quoteText: Do you use source control? Can you make a build in one step? Do you make daily builds? Do you have a bug database?

sources.title: Joel on Software — The Joel Test (August 9, 2000)
